From the archive: 30 October 1987, Manchester's independent brewers keep it real | Beer

Beer has followed wine in developing a global perspective. Once it was enough to rave about Greene King's Abbot Ale and Timothy Taylor's Landlord, just as wine fit to drink came from only three countries. But the smart set now moan about weakened purity laws, or scour the back end of Flanders for a beer rumoured to mash in a thermal spring before being sprinkled spontaneously with essence of syrup of figs.

The point about Germany, Belgium or Czechoslovakia is that beer rates as an item high on the agenda of many tourists. Would we could claim as much for Britain! As our brewers fall over themselves to promote lager, one wonders how long it will be before the traditional, top-fermented pint disappears.

A few strongholds survive to which drinking strangers can be directed with confidence, and one of them is Manchester. You work up a thirst clambering round the Peak District then hop across to the big city nearby for a good slake. This may shock the people paid to sell Manchester, since they rarely list beer among its attractions. If a readable pub guide exists, I missed it - there are CAMRA leaflets that are fine for explorers but hardly contribute much to tourism.

With Whitbread about to abandon their Salford brewery, all the nationals will now be trunking beer in from afar. That leaves six independents of substance. Most of them concentrate on local trade and this is certainly true of Hyde from Moss Side, the smallest brewery, with about 50 houses spread mainly in the south of the city. All sell their dry, sharp bitter and one or other mild.

Robinson of Stockport, the other South Manchester brewery, stretch well into Cheshire and Derbyshire. Their most central pub, the Castle in Oldham Street, makes a good choice to end a crawl because it usually serves Old Tom, pick of the strong dark winter beers that now seem to extend into other seasons like the winters themselves.

Boddington, a recent take-over target, have upset the purists, not so much because they are the most expansionist brewery around but because many believe the beer has suffered. Their bitter, as I recall, had a distinctive palate and a tangy aftertaste that made me think of peppermint. The palate remains full and fruity but the peppermint is no more.

What has probably happened is what afflicts other beers that enjoy national distribution. No logic in carting the stuff vast distances if customers at the other end object to the taste, so you remove anything that might arouse strong passions for or against. A useful comparison can be made with the Oldham Brewery, which Boddington acquired in 1982 and, to their credit, have kept open. Oldham's beers are confined to Manchester and simply erupt with flavour.

That is even truer of Joseph Holt. It has been alleged that several years ago they went through a bad patch, but the fault could lie with critics who, in the first flush of the keg revolution, had mislaid their tastebuds.

I well remember my introduction to Holt's bitter. It took an age to pour, as the pumps were so worn (Holt have never been knee-jerk refurbishers). Each tug of the handle advanced the cause by barely an inch. When I finally pressed glass to lips, the beer struck me as acrid and vinegary. How soon could I make my excuses and leave? But the more I drank, the better it tasted. Long before the glass was emptied, I was hooked.

John Willie Lees of Middleton Junction are odd ones out: whereas Manchester beers tend to be sharp, the bitter from Lees is exceptionally malty.

It does the heart good to visit a busy pub and watch drinkers from all the social grades knock back the milds and bitters. Anything chilled and yellow is not treated too seriously even by brewers, who either transpose trademarks into German - Amboss for Hyde's anvil; Einhorn for Robinson's unicorn - or invest their lagers with bastard Anglosprach like Holtenbrau. I ask you.
